catalog_quote: [p. 197] O acento em Krenak mostra-se como previsível, caindo sobre a última sílaba do item lexical isolado. [...] [p. 198] Como foi mencionado anteriormente, o acento primário da língua Krenak no item lexical isolado cai sistematicamente sobre a última sílaba da palavra. Apesar de não ser uma língua com sensibilidade ao peso silábico, deve-se ressaltar a grande tendência da língua a apresentar sílabas finais travadas ((C)VC), mas que recebem o acento indistintamente. [...] Quando o item é formado por três sílabas, entretanto, um acento secundário é atribuído. Assim, aplica-se o acento primário na última sílaba, mas a primeira sílaba passa a receber um acento secundário. [...] [p. 201] Assim, percebemos que em palavras com duas sílabas o acento cai sempre na última sílaba. Porém, se tiver três ou mais sílabas, o acento primário será na última, mas o acento secundário marcará a primeira sílaba da palavra. [...] [p. 204] É importante ressaltar que a língua não apresenta sensibilidade ao peso, podendo, portanto, sílabas leves ou pesadas receberem proeminência [...] de modo que a última sílaba, mesmo quando monomoráica (CV), sempre é acentuada.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: [p. 197] Stress in Krenak proves to be predictable, falling on the last syllable of the isolated lexical item. [...] [p. 198] As mentioned earlier, the primary stress of Krenak in the isolated lexical item falls systematically on the last syllable of the word. Although it is not a language sensitive to syllable weight, one should note the language's strong tendency to have closed final syllables ((C)VC), which however receive stress indiscriminately. [...] When the item consists of three syllables, however, a secondary stress is assigned. Thus primary stress applies to the last syllable, but the first syllable comes to receive a secondary stress.
new_statements.citation: Pessoa, Katia Nepomuceno. 2012. Análise fonética e fonológica da língua Krenak e abordagem preliminar de contos Botocudo. Tese de Doutorado em Linguística, IEL, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (orient. Lucy Seki).

Lucy Seki; downloaded from etnolinguistica.org). extracted text of p. 197 (printed 197) gives sec. 4.5.2 'O acento em Krenak': 'O acento em Krenak mostra-se como previsivel, caindo sobre a ultima silaba do item lexical isolado.' and the two numbered generalizations (1) predictable on the last syllable of the isolated lexical item, (2) stress changes in domains larger than the word. p. 198, sec. 4.5.2.1: 'o acento primario da lingua Krenak no item lexical isolado cai sistematicamente sobre a ultima s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (primary) stress is predictable and falls on the final syllable of the word in citation form, regardless of syllable weight (open CV/V finals and monosyllables are stressed just like closed finals); words of three or more syllables additionally carry a secondary stress on the initial syllable; the author analyses the system as quantity-insensitive iambs built left to right with the rightmost foot head as primary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of words with three or more syllables (Pessoa 2012 pp. 198, 201; following Silva 1986 p. 56, who describes it as perceptible mainly through greater duration than the second syllable); none in disyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions given. In domains larger than the word (phonological phrase, declarative sentence) stresses are readjusted: a word's lexical final primary stress may surface as secondary under the falling declarative contour (sec. 4.5.2.2, pp. 201-204; examples limited, footnote 34). Portuguese paroxytone loans lose their final unstressed syllable so that stress ends up word-final (p. 190). Silva 1986 (p. 58) adds that stressed syllables are always closed in her data, whereas Pessoa 2012 explicitly says open finals are stressed too.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly about the isolated lexical item (citation form); the author states that stress position is readjusted in the phonological word/phrase and sentence domain (rhythm and intonation), so final stress is a word-level generalization. No acoustic study of stress was carried out (impressionistic, with a few F0 tracks of sentences).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kren1239 'Borum' = Krenak (Krenák), the sole surviving Botocudo/Borum variety, ISO 639-3 kqq. Both Silva 1986 and Pessoa 2012 describe the speech of the last Krenak speakers of Aldeia Krenak on the Rio Doce (Resplendor/Conselheiro Pena, Minas Gerais) and of Krenak at Posto Vanuíre (SP); Pessoa's data are largely Seki's 1980s-2000s recordings plus her own. Part II of Pessoa 2012 concerns Manizer's 1915 Botocudo texts (same language, earlier stage).

new_statements.quote: Der Akzent liegt mit ganz vereinzelten Ausnahmen stets auf der letzten Silbe. Die Worte sind entweder einsilbige Wurzeln, oder aus solchen zusammengesetzt.
new_statements.translation: The accent lies, with quite isolated exceptions, always on the last syllable. The words are either monosyllabic roots, or compounded from such.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (rule 01/001/0001.., final) and as Pessoa 2012 (acento primário na última sílaba do item lexical isolado) and Silva 1986. Rudolph's data are from the Mucury district (Rio Mucury, Rio de Todos os Santos, São Mateus, Rio Preto), mostly the Nak-nenuk group per Seler's Vorwort, collected before 1902; he says he found no substantial linguistic differences among these groups. It adds nothing on secondary stress, weight or the phrasal domain; the only addition is the 1902-era observation itself, a century before the modern Krenak descriptions, plus the vague acknowledgement of rare exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is on the final syllable of the word; Rudolph notes only 'quite isolated' exceptions without naming any. He adds that words are monosyllabic roots or compounds of them, so final stress on a compound is stress on its last root.
new_statements.exceptions: 'mit ganz vereinzelten Ausnahmen' (with quite isolated exceptions); no exceptions are listed or characterised in the introduction. The dictionary entries themselves carry no stress marks (vowel-length/nasal diacritics only).
new_statements.identity_note: Rudolph 1909 describes the Botocudo spoken by the groups of the Mucury, Todos os Santos, São Mateus and Rio Preto forests (Minas Gerais / Espírito Santo), mainly the Nak-nenuk according to Seler's preface; he states that all these groups showed no essential linguistic differences. This is the 19th/early-20th-century ancestor of the Krenak variety described by Silva 1986 and Pessoa 2012, treated by Glottolog as the same language (kren1239, ISO kqq). Araújo 1992 is, per its PuRe metadata, an analysis of Rudolph's dictionary rather than new field data.

new_statements.quote: [p. 57] 3. O diacrítico " ʼ " ao que se pode supor, foi usado em certas circunstâncias para indicar o acento. Na Introdução ao Wörterbuch (p.VI), Rudolph menciona que o acento estava normalmente na última sílaba, salvo poucas exceções. Observam-se no Wörterbuch ocorrências do diacrítico " ʼ " na penúltima sílaba da palavra, casos em que foi provavelmente usado para assinalar que se tratava de exceções à norma geral, sob o ponto de vista da percepção de Rudolph. [p. 58] (25) a) aminkáki "flor" b) hararáte "cansado" c) bekáne "abelha"
new_statements.translation: [p. 57] 3. The diacritic ' ʼ ', as far as one can suppose, was used in certain circumstances to indicate the accent. In the Introduction to the Wörterbuch (p. VI), Rudolph mentions that the accent was normally on the last syllable, with few exceptions. In the Wörterbuch one observes occurrences of the diacritic ' ʼ ' on the penultimate syllable of the word, cases in which it was probably used to signal that these were exceptions to the general norm, from the point of view of Rudolph's perception. [p. 58] (25) a) aminkáki 'flower' b) hararáte 'tired' c) bekáne 'bee'.

Wörterbuch der Botokudensprache'), not new field data. It adds one detail: names three of Rudolph's exception words with a penultimate acute (aminkáki, hararáte, bekáne).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent in Rudolph's Naknanuk (Botocudo) material falls normally on the final syllable; Araújo restates Rudolph's own p. VI statement and interprets Rudolph's acute diacritic on a penultimate vowel (aminkáki, hararáte, bekáne) as marking the few lexical exceptions with penultimate accent, while noting the same mark is elsewhere used for hiatus (moí, maín), for the non-syllabic status of an adjacent vowel (japokoé, koém, hingoé) and possibly for mid-vowel aperture. No independent stress analysis of new field data is offered (philological study).
new_statements.exceptions: 'salvo poucas exceções': words carrying Rudolph's acute mark on the penult, e.g. aminkáki 'flor', hararáte 'cansado', bekáne 'abelha' (printed p. 58, ex. 25), read as exceptional penultimate accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Araújo's dissertation is a philological analysis of Bruno Rudolph's 1909 Wörterbuch, collected among the Naknanuk subgroup of the Botocudo (forests along the Mucuri, Todos os Santos, São Mateus and Preto rivers, Minas Gerais), using modern Krenak/Nakrehé (Seki's and Silva's data) and other Botocudo word lists as controls; the stress remark concerns Rudolph's Naknanuk material, a historical variety subsumed under Glottolog kren1239 (Krenak/Botocudo).

tone.quote: Der Wortakzent im Krenák ist fest und fällt bei einem frei stehenden Lexem systematisch auf die letzte Silbe. Dies ist typisch für Sprachen des Macro-Jê Stammes. Das Krenák verfügt über Lexeme mit ein, zwei oder drei Silben (Silva 1986:56). Dreisilbige Lexeme erhalten einen sekundären Wortakzent auf der ersten Silbe, wie folgendes Beispiel zeigt: (3) [ˈm̥ak] ‘perna’ [ʒi.ˈɾubm] ‘branco, claro’ [ˌku.pa.ˈɾak] ‘onça’
tone.locator: p. 27, last paragraph of sec. 4.2.1 'Phonetische und phonologische Aspekte des Krenák' (pp. 24-27), immediately before 4.2.2; example (3) follows the paragraph
tone.translation: Word accent in Krenák is fixed and, on a free-standing lexeme, falls systematically on the last syllable. This is typical of languages of the Macro-Jê stock. Krenák has lexemes of one, two or three syllables (Silva 1986:56). Trisyllabic lexemes receive a secondary word accent on the first syllable, as the following example shows: (3) [ˈm̥ak] 'leg', [ʒi.ˈɾubm] 'white, light', [ˌku.pa.ˈɾak] 'jaguar'.
